action.description: Action object MUST contain a field `submission`, and MAY contain arbitrary additional information.

actTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) to obtain an action from an agent.

includeLegalActions.description: If true, include legalActions and legalActionStrings in observations. Defaults to false since these can be derived from serializedGameAndState.

initialActions.description: Actions applied to initial state before play begins to set up starting position.

loadPresetHands.description: Repeated poker only. Load preset hand chance actions from preset_hands.jsonl.

openSpielGameName.description: The short_name of the OpenSpiel game to load.

openSpielGameParameters.description: Game parameters for Open Spiel game.

openSpielGameString.description: The full game string including parameters.

presetHands.description: Repeated poker only. List of per-hand chance action sequences to use instead of random chance.

runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The game is in its opening move. Opponent (x) has claimed the bottom-center cell, which is the single most valuable starting square in Connect Four because it participates in the largest number of possible 4-in-a-row lines (horizontal, vertical, and both diagonal directions). As second player I must therefore fight for the same central file before the opponent can occupy more cells in it; dropping in column 3 places my disk directly above the existing x, seizes continuing control of the center, and keeps all of my future options (vertical stack, diagonals left or right) maximally flexible. Any other column at this stage would cede the center for free and allow x an immediate follow-up in column 3 that would be harder to answer later.

Final Answer: 3

The strongest plan here is to expand on the bottom row next to your existing center disc. Dropping in column 2 lands an **x** at (row 5, col 2), giving you an immediate horizontal **xx** on the bottom (cols 2–3). This is the most forcing continuation because it sets up the very dangerous idea of later forming **xxx** on the bottom with two playable winning ends (a classic double-threat), and it also keeps play in the high-value central area. action.thoughts:
The current position is early-game with minimal material (only 3 disks placed total). Opponent holds a modest horizontal duo at the bottom of columns 2-3; my existing disk sits directly atop the column-3 x. No immediate threats, forks, or 3-in-a-row exist for either side, so the objective is long-term positional control.

In Connect Four, occupying the central file (column 3) maximizes future winning lines (vertical, both diagonals) while restricting the opponent's ability to build through the middle. Dropping here continues the vertical stack in the highest-value column without allowing the opponent an easy central reply. Peripheral or blocking moves (e.g., column 2 or 4) are playable but cede the direct center and create fewer simultaneous threats on the subsequent turn.

Thus the move that preserves the strongest minimax evaluation is to extend the center column.

Final Answer: 3
